summary: Fills a gap in the IPv6 socket APIs by adding socket options and getaddrinfo flags that let applications influence source address selection. It builds on RFC 3484 default address selection. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 5014 lets an IPv6 application ask the system to prefer a certain kind of source address. If that kind is unavailable, the system can use its normal selection rules instead.

questions: ipv6 socket api source address selection
how to choose source address ipv6
how to prefer temporary ipv6 source address
subtitle: IPv6 socket options that let applications express source-address preferences

tldr.problem: IPv6 default address-selection rules offer no basic socket API for applications to express some source-address preferences.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5014 defines the IPV6_ADDR_PREFERENCES socket option and getaddrinfo flags for choosing among home, care-of, temporary, public, CGA, and non-CGA addresses.
tldr.outcome: The API expresses preferences, not guarantees. Applications that require a particular address type can select and validate the chosen address.

today: RFC 5014 is an Informational API document published in September 2007. The supplied metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Applications Need Address Preferences
sections.content:
RFC 3484 defines default rules for choosing IPv6 source addresses. An application may want a different preference, such as using a temporary address or a Care-of Address, without implementing all address-selection rules itself.

RFC 5014 lets an application state a preference and leaves the remaining selection to the system. The preference is a request rather than a requirement: if no matching address is available, the system may choose another address.
sections.plainLanguage: An application can ask the system to prefer a type of IPv6 address. The system still makes the final choice and can use another address if needed.

sections.title: Preference Flags and the Socket Option
sections.content:
The RFC defines six flags: prefer home or care-of, temporary or public, and CGA or non-CGA source addresses. Each pair expresses opposite preferences; setting both flags in a pair is contradictory.

The IPV6_ADDR_PREFERENCES socket option carries the flags as a 32-bit unsigned integer. It applies to packets sent through that socket. Setting contradictory flags with setsockopt() results in EINVAL.
sections.plainLanguage: The application selects from three pairs of opposite preferences. It can set one preference in each pair or leave the system default in place.

sections.title: Using Preferences with getaddrinfo
sections.content:
The application can pass the same address preferences to getaddrinfo() so destination addresses are ordered with the requested source preference in mind. It sets AI_EXTFLAGS in ai_flags and places the preference flags in ai_eflags.

The application should use semantically equivalent preferences with getaddrinfo() and the socket option. If the getaddrinfo flags contain opposite preferences, the call fails with EAI_BADEXTFLAGS.
sections.plainLanguage: The application can tell both the address lookup and the socket which source address it prefers. Matching preferences keep the lookup order and packet sending behavior consistent.

sections.title: When an Application Needs a Specific Address
sections.content:
A preference alone cannot guarantee an address type. An application that must use a particular kind can select a source address for a destination, read the selected address, and check whether it meets the requirement.

The RFC defines bind2addrsel() to bind a socket to the source address that would be selected for a destination, and inet6_is_srcaddr() to validate address preferences. A specific address chosen with bind() or IPV6_PKTINFO takes precedence over the preference option.
sections.plainLanguage: When a program must use a certain address type, it needs to check the selected address before communicating. A preference by itself does not guarantee the result.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says the API has the security implications of the basic IPv6 socket API and the default address-selection rules. Letting an application prefer temporary addresses allows it to use their privacy properties on a per-application or per-socket basis.

Some preference settings, such as avoiding temporary or CGA addresses, may be restricted to privileged processes because of their security implications.
sections.plainLanguage: Address preferences can affect privacy and security. A system may limit some choices to trusted applications.
